transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Amy Held.
The G20 gathering has ended in Atlanta without a joint communique and no real consensus over
what to do about food and energy security hurt by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
NPR's Michelle Kellerman reports Secretary of State Marco Rubio was the host.
Secretary Rubio says the U.S. wants the G20 to focus on global economic stability, but
Russia's war against Ukraine and the U.S. war against Iran are still roiling food and
energy markets.
And Rubio is not ruling out a new round of strikes in Iran.
>> And the president's preference in any challenge around the world is to try to solve it diplomatically
and peacefully if possible.
He recognizes there are some issues in the world that cannot be solved peacefully, unfortunately,
sadly.
>> Many met on the sidelines with Russia's foreign minister to talk about Ukraine.
It's not clear if Russian president Vladimir Putin will attend the G20 summit in Florida
next month, but Trump could meet with him at an international gathering in China before
then.
Michelle Kellerman, NPR News, Atlanta.
>> Traditionally, younger voters turn out at disproportionately lower rates in midterms.
This year, cost of living is the top issue for voters, and polling shows younger voters
are experiencing more financial insecurity.
Now college students are making up a growing voter block.
But campuses are polarized, and NPR's Janet Ujung Lee reports on efforts to discuss politics
there.
>> In her first year at the University of Michigan, Sarah Katherine Jackson had a hard
time finding her political home.
>> I had some ideas that I agreed with the college Republicans.
I had some ideas that I disagreed with them, and I felt like I couldn't voice those disagreements
in that setting.
Same with college Democrats.
I couldn't voice my disagreements with the Democratic Party.
>> Jackson says the meetings felt like an echo chamber with no room for discussion until
she found a newer political organization called Bridge USA.
>> They're the tragic assassination of Charlie Kirk.
You have campus violence, and importantly, students are now telling us that we need dialogue
because our lives depend on it.
>> Manu Meel is the co-founder of Bridge USA.
Its mission is to get progressives and conservatives to talk to each other.
Janet Ujung Lee, NPR News.
>> A federal judge in Massachusetts has ruled against part of the Trump administration's
plan for people on Medicaid to prove they are working.
As NPR's Selena Simmons Duffin reports, states are being told to put work requirements in
effect January 1st.
>> A coalition of Democratic state attorneys general sued the Trump administration in June
over its work requirement rules, which required Medicaid beneficiaries with conditions like
HIV or cancer to prove that their condition made them unable to work.
A federal judge agreed that the Trump administration went beyond the text of the law passed by
Congress and vacated that part of the guidelines while otherwise allowing the Medicaid work
requirements to take effect in January.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services declined to comment about whether the agency
would appeal the ruling.
Selena Simmons Duffin, NPR News.
>> It's NPR News.
Road watches are in effect this weekend for the southwestern Four Corners area, where
New Mexico, Colorado, Arizona, and Utah meet.
The region has dealt with heavy rain for weeks and more is forecast, leading to the potential
for flash flooding.
Some residents have already been displaced, and the Navajo reservation has been especially
hard hit.
At least one person died in flooding last weekend.
Tomorrow marks the end of daylight saving time.
Most Americans will turn their clocks back one hour at 2 a.m. local.
NPR's Ava Berger reports like clockwork controversy over the time change has come up again.
>> An extra hour of sleep is just a day away.
At 2 a.m. Sunday morning, many clocks across the country will be sent backwards one hour.
This twice yearly change has once again become political.
According to a Gallup poll from last year, more than half of Americans want daylight
saving time gone, President Donald Trump agrees.
He wants to make daylight saving time permanent.
That means the clocks won't change.
Here's what he told auto workers during a July speech in Michigan.
>> Let's get rid of daylight saving time stuff, okay?
>> A bipartisan bill to do just that, the Sunshine Protection Act, is stuck in the Senate.
So tomorrow, the clocks will still jump back.
Ava Berger, NPR News.
>> The Youth Olympic Games opened in Senegal today, the first Olympic event in Africa.
About 2,700 athletes ages 14 to 17 compete through November 13.
Russia's delegation is competing under its national flag for the first time at an Olympic
event since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
It's NPR News.

topics.text: G20 meeting in Atlanta ends without joint communique on food and energy security
Secretary Rubio does not rule out new strikes in Iran, prefers diplomacy
Russia's foreign minister meets G20 counterparts on sidelines to discuss Ukraine
Bridge USA works to get progressives and conservatives talking on college campuses
Federal judge blocks part of Trump Medicaid work requirement rules, others take effect January
Flash flood watches in effect for Four Corners region after weeks of heavy rain
Daylight saving time ends Sunday; Trump pushes permanent time, bill stalled in Senate
Youth Olympic Games open in Senegal, first Olympic event held in Africa
